description: Psilocybe cubensis is a psilocybin-producing mushroom in the family Hymenogastraceae, recognized by its golden-brown to caramel cap, dark purple-brown spore print, and the blue bruising of its flesh where handled. It is a dung-loving (coprophilous) species of warm grasslands and is the most widely cultivated of the "magic mushrooms." This profile is educational/informational only.
edibilityNotes: Contains the controlled psychoactive tryptamines psilocybin and psilocin and is illegal to possess or cultivate in most jurisdictions. Not a culinary food; ingestion produces hallucinogenic effects. Critical safety risk: misidentification with toxic dung- and grass-inhabiting species (e.g. Galerina, Conocybe/Pholiotina) that contain deadly amatoxins. Educational information only — do not consume.
distribution: Pantropical and subtropical, occurring across the Americas (notably the Gulf Coast of the United States, Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean, and South America), Southeast Asia, and Australia.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Galerina marginata
dangerousLookalikes.note: A deadly amatoxin-containing mushroom. It grows on wood/lignin (decaying logs, buried wood) rather than dung, has a rusty-brown (not purple-brown) spore print, and does NOT stain blue. Any brown-spored, non-bluing mushroom in this size class should be treated as potentially deadly.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Conocybe / Pholiotina species
dangerousLookalikes.note: Small brown dung- and grass-inhabiting mushrooms; some (e.g. Pholiotina rugosa, formerly Conocybe filaris) contain deadly amatoxins. They have rusty- to cinnamon-brown spore prints, fragile stems, and do not bruise blue.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Panaeolus / other Psilocybe species
dangerousLookalikes.note: Other coprophilous psilocybin and non-psilocybin mushrooms share dung habitat and dark spore prints; precise distinction requires microscopy and spore color, and non-bluing brown-spored species may be toxic.
